title: Attention residue
hook: part of the mind stays on the last task after the switch (Leroy)

segments.voice: Yesterday, switching costs, and the line one at a time. How did the batches go? Did the messages wait, or did they win? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

The meeting ended ten minutes ago. The body has moved on: new room, new screen, new task. But a sentence from the meeting is still playing. What did she mean by that? Should I have said something? The report in front of you gets read, and read again, and somehow nothing goes in. Yesterday was about the cost of the switch itself. Today is about what lingers after it, the part of the mind that didn't get the memo that we moved. A researcher named Sophie Leroy gave that leftover a name, and it's today's word.
screen: `THE MEETING IS OVER.` → `THE SENTENCE IS STILL PLAYING.` → `THE REPORT WON'T GO IN.`

segments.voice: First, the finding. Leroy studied what happens when people leave one task and start another. She found that thoughts about the first task kept running in the background, and that people with more of those leftover thoughts did worse on the next task. She called it attention residue: some of your attention stays stuck to the thing you just left. Second, what makes it stickier. In her studies, residue was stronger when the first task was left unfinished. A half-done job keeps tapping on the shoulder. When people finished the first task, especially under a little time pressure that pushed them to close it out, the residue was lower. Third, a way to loosen it. In later work, Leroy and a colleague tested something simple: before switching, people wrote a quick plan for where they would pick the task back up. That small note seemed to help the mind let go, as if it trusted the plan to remember so it didn't have to. Fourth, an old echo. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius, in his private notebook, kept urging himself to give full attention to the thing in hand, and to set aside every other thought while doing it. He had no lab and no word for residue. But he knew the problem: the mind trailing behind the body, still in the last room. The research doesn't say you can switch without any leftover. It suggests the leftover can be made smaller, by finishing what you can, and writing down what you can't.
screen: `THE LAST TASK KEEPS RUNNING.` · `UNFINISHED WORK STICKS HARDER.` · then, large: `WRITE WHERE YOU'LL PICK IT UP.` · then: `THE THING IN HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a pause between tasks. Bring back whatever you were doing just before this. If it's unfinished, say silently, in one short sentence, where you'll pick it up. Next I'll call the landlord. Next I'll fix page three. That's the note. Now set it down. For the sit, let the breath be the new room you've walked into. When the last task tugs, don't fight it. Notice it, remind yourself the note has it, and come back. The bell holds the time.
Attention residue. The part of the mind that stays on the last task after you've moved to the next one. Today's word.

Your line: clear the residue. Today, at the end of each task, take ten seconds: finish one small piece, or write one line about where you'll start next time. Then begin the next thing. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: People who use this research often close each task with a short note on where to resume, or take a brief pause between meetings before starting the next thing.

residue was stronger when the first task was left unfinished
a half-done job kept more attention stuck to it.

fork.setup: you have to leave a report half finished and jump into a meeting. what helps the residue most, by Leroy's later work?
options: promise yourself you'll stop thinking about it.
write a quick line on where you'll pick it back up.
keep the report open on a second screen.
fork.reveal: a short plan for where to resume seemed to help the mind let go of the unfinished task.

trapdoor: what you thought: when you switch tasks, your mind switches too.
what it means: part of your attention stays on the last task, and the next one suffers for it.
what a scholar hears: Leroy found residue stronger after unfinished tasks; a later study found a quick resume plan reduced it.

sources.ref: Leroy, "Why is it so hard to do my work? The challenge of attention residue when switching between work tasks"

notes: Index hook carried a year (Leroy, 2009); the script leaves it out under the claims rule.
Confirm the summary of Leroy's findings: residue higher after unfinished tasks; lower when the first task was finished under time pressure.
Confirm Leroy & Glomb's 'ready-to-resume plan' finding and its full citation.
